subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: How many three-letter strings with distinct letters can be formed from five distinct letters?
solution_latex: Order matters and repetition is forbidden, so ${}^5P_3=5\cdot4\cdot3=60$.
common_mistake: Using ${5\choose3}$ ignores the order of the letters.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: Two fair dice are rolled. What is $P(\text{sum}=7)$?
solution_latex: The six ordered pairs $(1,6),\ldots,(6,1)$ work out of 36 equally likely pairs, giving $6/36=1/6$.
common_mistake: Treating unordered pairs as equally likely changes the sample space.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: If $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive with $P(A)=0.3$ and $P(B)=0.4$, then $P(A\cup B)$ is
solution_latex: Mutual exclusivity gives $P(A\cap B)=0$, so $P(A\cup B)=0.3+0.4=0.7$.
common_mistake: Multiplying applies to independent intersections, not disjoint unions.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: Which set must be an event in every probability model?
options: Both the empty set and sample space
Every subset, even for an arbitrary sigma-algebra
solution_latex: Every sigma-algebra contains $\varnothing$ and $\Omega$. It need not contain every subset when $\Omega$ is uncountable.
common_mistake: A sample space does not force the power set to be the event collection.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: For any event $A$ with $P(A)=0.27$, $P(A^c)$ equals
common_mistake: The complement is subtracted from one, not from the sample size.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: Ten people form a committee of three. How many committees are possible?
solution_latex: Membership has no roles, so use ${10\choose3}=120$.
common_mistake: A committee is unordered; permutations overcount each committee by $3!$.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: Which statements are always true for events $A,B$?
solution_latex: Intersection is contained in $A$, union contains $A$, and complementation gives the last identity. Additivity without subtraction requires disjointness.
common_mistake: Do not use the disjoint-union formula without the disjointness condition.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: If independent events $A,B$ satisfy $P(A)=1/2$ and $P(A\cup B)=3/4$, then $P(B)$ is
common_mistake: Independence determines the intersection, not the union directly.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: Which pair of events from one fair die roll is independent?
solution_latex: $P(A)=1/2$, $P(B)=1/3$, and $P(A\cap B)=P(\{1\})=1/6=P(A)P(B)$, so the second pair is independent.
common_mistake: Always verify the product rule exactly.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: A password has two distinct letters followed by two distinct digits. Reuse is forbidden within each group. The count is
solution_latex: Positions are ordered: $26P2\times10P2=26\cdot25\cdot10\cdot9$.
common_mistake: Choosing unordered letter/digit sets loses positional order.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: How many binary strings of length 8 contain exactly three ones?
solution_latex: ${8\choose3}=56$: choose the three positions occupied by ones.
common_mistake: Do not arrange the chosen ones again; they are identical.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: How many nonnegative integer solutions satisfy $x+y+z=10$?
solution_latex: Stars and bars gives ${12\choose2}=66$.
common_mistake: Nonnegative solutions use $n+k-1$ positions; positive solutions use a shifted total.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: How many positive integer solutions satisfy $x_1+x_2+x_3+x_4=10$?
solution_latex: Set $y_i=x_i-1\ge0$. Then $\sum y_i=6$, giving ${9\choose3}=84$.
common_mistake: Account for the mandatory one in every variable before applying stars and bars.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: From 7 men and 5 women, how many 4-person committees contain exactly 2 women?
solution_latex: Choose independently: ${5\choose2}{7\choose2}=10\cdot21=210$.
common_mistake: The order of committee members is irrelevant.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: A fair coin is tossed 5 times. Enter $32P(\text{at least one head})$.
solution_latex: $P(\text{no heads})=1/32$, so the requested scaled probability is $32(31/32)=31$.
common_mistake: “At least one” is fastest through its complement.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: Events $A,B$ have $P(A)=0.6$, $P(B)=0.5$, and $P(A\cup B)=0.8$. Enter $10P(A\cap B)$.
solution_latex: Inclusion–exclusion gives $P(A\cap B)=0.6+0.5-0.8=0.3$; scaling gives 3.
common_mistake: Subtract the union; do not assume independence.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: A box contains 4 red, 3 blue, and 2 green balls. Two are drawn without replacement. How many unordered pairs have different colors?
solution_latex: Count cross-color pairs: $4\cdot3+4\cdot2+3\cdot2=12+8+6=26$.
common_mistake: Within a cross-color pair there is no extra factor of two.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: How many onto functions exist from a 3-element set to a 2-element set?
solution_latex: There are $2^3=8$ functions; exclude the two constant functions, leaving 6.
common_mistake: Onto excludes functions that miss either codomain element.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: A fair die is rolled twice. Enter $36P(\text{the second result exceeds the first})$.
solution_latex: There are ${6\choose2}=15$ ordered increasing pairs among 36 outcomes.
common_mistake: The six ties prevent a simple one-half of all 36 outcomes.

subject: probability-statistics
question_latex: In a class of 30, 18 know Python, 14 know SQL, and 5 know neither. How many know both?
common_mistake: Convert “neither” into the union size first.
